title: Learn a word, then see it everywhere

lines.text: You learn a new word, and suddenly you see it everywhere.
Same with a car you just bought. Now it's on every road.
It isn't the world changing. It's your brain.
It's called the frequency illusion, a name coined by Stanford linguist Arnold Zwicky.
It's also known as the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon, after a reader's letter to a Minnesota newspaper in 1994.
Two things cause it. Selective attention: your brain now filters for that thing.
And confirmation bias: every time you spot it, you feel more sure it's everywhere.
It was always there. You just weren't looking.
And now that you know about it, you'll start noticing it everywhere.

sources.claim: Frequency illusion (Baader–Meinhof phenomenon): named by Arnold Zwicky in 2005; Baader-Meinhof name from a 1994 letter to the St. Paul Pioneer Press; caused by selective attention and confirmation bias
